title: Ksitigarbha's vow
hook: the bodhisattva vows not to rest until the hell realms are empty

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Medicine Buddha, deep blue, with vows for the sick who have no one. Your line: the healing Buddha. Who did you send a line to? Day one thousand two hundred.

Until the hells are empty, I will not become a Buddha. That's the vow, in the short form it's carried in, of a bodhisattva named Ksitigarbha. A promise usually comes with an end in sight: until the project's done, until the kids are grown, until the debt is paid. This one is built so that the end may never come. And the one who made it, in the story his sutra tells, started out as a grieving daughter. Today: Ksitigarbha's vow.
screen: `UNTIL THE HELLS ARE EMPTY.` → `A PROMISE WITH NO END IN SIGHT.` → `IT BEGINS WITH A DAUGHTER.`

segments.voice: The Sutra of Ksitigarbha's Original Vows tells several stories of his past lives. Here's one. Long ago, in the time of an earlier Buddha, there lived a young woman of a brahmin family. She was devoted and kind. Her mother was not. Her mother mocked the teaching and the Buddha, and then she died. The daughter was afraid of where her mother's actions would carry her. So she sold what she had, made offerings, and gave herself to devotion to the Buddha of that age, calling on him with her whole heart. And in the sutra's telling, she was taken to the edge of the hell realms, a sea of suffering, and she saw what was there. A guardian there told her that her mother had already been freed, because of the merit of her daughter's devotion. Her mother was safe. And here is the turn. She didn't go home relieved. She had seen everyone else still down there. So she vowed, before that Buddha, to spend lifetimes freeing every being who suffered in those places. That young woman, the sutra says, became Ksitigarbha. A private grief, for one person, opens out into a promise for everyone. Ksitigarbha is the bodhisattva who goes down, into the lowest places, the ones others would rather not look at. In art he is often a monk with a shaved head, holding a staff with rings and a jewel; some say the staff opens the gates and the jewel lights up the dark. Some read the vow as Ksitigarbha holding back his own awakening. Others hear it differently: that his awakening and everyone else's are tied together, and he won't untie them.
screen: `A DAUGHTER FEARS FOR HER MOTHER.` · `SHE SEES THE LOW PLACES.` · `ONE GRIEF BECOMES A VOW.` · `A STAFF, AND A LIGHT IN THE DARK.` · then, large: `NOT UNTIL ALL ARE FREE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice, if you'd like: stay with someone in a low place. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind someone in a place most people would rather not look at. A person sleeping in a doorway. Someone in prison. A relative the family has stopped calling. See them as clearly as you can. Notice the pull to look away, to think of something else. Don't fight it. Just come back, and stay with them for one more breath, then another. You don't have to empty anything today. The bell holds the time.
Ksitigarbha's vow. The bodhisattva's promise not to become a Buddha until the hell realms are empty. Today's word.
Your line: not until all are free. Today, when you see someone others walk past, don't look away. Meet their eyes, or say hello. Day one thousand two hundred.

howItsDone: In Chinese, Korean, Vietnamese and Japanese Buddhism, Ksitigarbha is honored as the bodhisattva of the lower realms, and his sutra is often recited for parents and loved ones who have died.
